summary: J. R. Hicks's 1935 Econometrica survey reviews recent progress in the theory of monopoly, organized under simple monopoly, monopolistic competition, and bilateral monopoly. It covers Cournot's foundations, the marginal revenue and marginal cost conditions, factor demand under monopoly, joint production and discrimination, and the Chamberlin-Robinson group equilibrium with its critique. The excerpt ends as the discussion of duopoly begins, with Cournot, Bertrand and Edgeworth.
one_line: J. R. Hicks's 1935 Econometrica survey of recent monopoly theory, covering simple monopoly, monopolistic competition and duopoly.
key_facts: The survey was published in Econometrica, Vol. 3, No. 1 (January 1935), pp. 1-20, by J. R. Hicks.
Hicks says the last five or six years saw at least four important works devoted to monopoly: those of Dr. Zeuthen, Dr. Schneider, Professor Chamberlin, and Mrs. Robinson.
Hicks states that the phenomena of monopolistic competition 'are not new phenomena; they were observed and analyzed, however imperfectly, by older economists, by Cairnes and Wicksell.'
The controversy on the 'Laws of Returns' was begun by Mr. Sraffa in 1926.
Hicks writes that Marshall's device of 'external economies' 'would not bear the weight that had been imposed upon it.'
Hicks divides the modern theory under three headings: (1) Simple monopoly, (2) Monopolistic Competition, and (3) Bilateral Monopoly.
For a monopolist with profit xf(x) - phi(x), the first-order condition is marginal revenue equals marginal cost, and Hicks notes that Mrs. Robinson named marginal revenue.
Hicks states that the elasticity of demand relates to marginal revenue as marginal revenue = price times (1 - 1/elasticity).
Hicks writes that the best of all monopoly profits is 'a quiet life.'

Hicks states that Chamberlin concludes analysis based on perfect competition makes 'the price always too low, the cost of production too low, the scale of production too large, and the number of producers too small.'
Hicks says that under monopolistic competition equilibrium is only possible when average costs are diminishing.
Hicks notes that Professor Hotelling demonstrated in 'Stability in Competition' a tendency for two firms competing for a market to get together in the centre of the market.
Hicks says that once there are more than two firms in the market, 'they will tend to scatter, since any firm will try to avoid being caught between a pair of others.'
Hicks attributes the classical duopoly theory to Cournot, with criticisms by Bertrand and Edgeworth forming its 'ancient history'.
Hicks credits Amoroso and Wicksell with leading a post-war renaissance of Cournotism.
